doc.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview

chapter: Flip Benson, Grand Rapids and the Army
title: Detroit and joining Flip Benson's band in 1939
summary: Ware plays one night in Detroit, then receives a telegram from Flip Benson, an arranger-leader; he gets his first tuxedo and learns discipline.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: over, and I went to Detroit to play with some guys -- we went in the place of the Cats and Fiddles. The Cats and Fiddles had another gig, and they wanted us to play in their place as the Cats and Fiddles -- which we did. A place called the 12 Horsemen Club. Just for one night we played.

And I come back to Chicago and there was a telegram from a fellow named Flip Benson, this is 1939 -- and Flip had a 6 piece band, alto, tenor, trombone, bass, drum and piano. And Flip was what you would call a real musician; to me, everything they played was arranged -- he did the arranging. Flip is still alive now, I'm happy to say. I was in contact with him not too long ago, although I heard he just had a stroke, but the alto player, Charles Copeland is still alive out on the West Coast -- I've been in touch with him. But that's when I learned discipline.

We played nothing but the white clubs. I went back to Quincy with him because Bob Crist told him about me and that he needed a bass player, and he sent for me. I still got the telegram. I think my salary was to start was $21 or $22 a week, to start. And he gave me a raise periodically. And he treated me just like a son. See, that was in 1939. Yeah, the summer of 1939, and I went down and that's when I wore my first tuxedo. You know, I had been dressing in zoot suits and what not, but a tux, a dinner jacket, with black tuxedo pants -- and I thought I was something.
